module.title: Unit 3: What's in a Name?: Present Perfect with Already & Yet
module.objective: Mampu memberikan nasihat, mengungkapkan kewajiban, dan memberikan larangan menggunakan modal verbs (have to, ought to, should, must, had better, can't). Memahami dan menggunakan ekspresi idiomatik terkait 'name' dalam konteks komunikasi sehari-hari.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: What's in a Name and Brand?
subModules.grammarFocus: Modal Verbs of Obligation, Advice, and Prohibition (have to, should, must, had better, can't)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Business and naming vocabulary related to brands, consumers, and identity

content.summary: Welcome to the reading module for Unit 3. In this lesson, you will explore how companies choose names for their brands and products, and how rules and advice apply when making important naming decisions. You will practice reading strategies such as scanning for modal verbs and extracting specific details from business texts.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Modal verbs for obligation, advice, and prohibition (have to, should, ought to, must, had better, can't).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Terms related to commerce, branding, consumer habits, and personal identity.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning text for modal verbs and specific advisory phrases to understand author intent and guidelines.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of short B2 texts about product branding and naming conventions.
Locate specific advice and obligations expressed through modal verbs in written passages.
Recognize and apply vocabulary related to manufacturers, consumers, and logos in context.

contextWarmup.prompt: When a company creates a new product, what is the most important factor in choosing its name?
options: It must be easy to remember and unique in the market.
It has to be the exact name of the company owner.
It should be written in a foreign language to confuse consumers.
contextWarmup.explanation: A successful brand name needs to be memorable and distinctive so consumers can easily recognize it among competitors.

rules: Use 'have to' and 'don't have to' to talk about external rules and lack of obligation: You have to register the brand name legally. You don't have to use a family name.
Use 'should', 'shouldn't', and 'ought to' to give advice and recommendations: You should choose a short name. A brand name ought to be easy to understand.
Use 'must' and 'mustn't' for strong internal obligation and strict prohibitions: You must protect your trademark. You mustn't copy another company's logo.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Lack of Obligation with Prohibition
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up 'don't have to' (meaning it is not necessary) with 'mustn't' (meaning it is forbidden).
commonTrap.wrong: You mustn't use a short name if you want a long one.
commonTrap.correct: You don't have to use a short name, but you can if you prefer.

content.passageTitle: The Rules of Branding Your Business
paragraphs: When starting a new business venture, every manufacturer has to face a crucial challenge. You must choose a brand name that captures consumer attention immediately. According to marketing experts, a brand name ought to be unique, memorable, and easy to pronounce across different languages and cultures. If you fail to research global meanings, your product might face unexpected disasters in foreign markets.

Furthermore, retail chains and modern companies cannot succeed simply by selling standard goods. They have to build a strong corporate identity, which includes designing a recognizable logo and running targeted advertisements. Consumers are very observant, and they want products that reflect their personal values. Therefore, business owners had better invest time and effort into branding before launching any new commercial campaign.

questions.question: What advice is given to business owners regarding branding before launching campaigns?

content.summary: Listen for key information about obligations and peer pressure in everyday teenage conversations. Focus on modal verbs such as must, have to, and should to understand speaker intent and speaker attitude.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about school pressure and phones.
Identify details such as rules, obligations, and personal preferences.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during fast dialogues.

keyPhrases.note: The social stress to act or dress like friends of the same age group.
The newest item released by a brand.
A famous name associated with a company or manufacturer.
To decide between two or more options.

connectedSpeech.note: The final /t/ in must links directly into the vowel sound of get.
The word to reduces its vowel sound to a schwa /ə/.
Assimilation occurs when /t/ and /d/ combine with /j/ to form /dʒ/.
The preposition to becomes weak when spoken quickly in natural conversation.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Naming Rules and Modal Obligations

content.summary: Master modal verbs of obligation, advice, and prohibition such as have to, should, must, and had better when writing about naming conventions and rules.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Expressing Strong Obligation and Prohibition
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + must / have to / mustn't / can't + base verb
blueprintItems.example: You must give the product a unique name before launching it.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Giving Advice and Recommendations
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + should / ought to / shouldn't + base verb
blueprintItems.example: A brand name ought to be memorable and easy to understand.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Delivering Urgent Warnings
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + had better / had better not + base verb
blueprintItems.example: You had better check trademark laws before registering your business name.

mechanicsRules.rule: Never add an 's' to modal verbs in the third person singular.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He musts register the company name today.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He must register the company name today.
mechanicsRules.why: Modal verbs like must, should, and can do not take an 's' in the third person.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always follow modal verbs directly with the bare infinitive without 'to', except for 'ought to'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You should to choose a shorter name.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: You should choose a shorter name.
mechanicsRules.why: Most modals require the base form of the verb without the particle 'to'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Distinguish between absence of obligation and prohibition.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You mustn't use a family name if you prefer a modern brand.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: You don't have to use a family name if you prefer a modern brand.
mechanicsRules.why: Mustn't expresses strict prohibition, whereas don't have to means something is optional.

sampleSentences.en: You have to give the new product a memorable name.
sampleSentences.id: Kamu harus memberi nama produk baru itu dengan nama yang mudah diingat.

sampleSentences.en: A brand name ought to be unique and clear.
sampleSentences.id: Sebuah nama merek seharusnya unik dan jelas.

sampleSentences.en: You can't call your twins unusual names that cause embarrassment.
sampleSentences.id: Kamu tidak boleh memanggil anak kembarmu dengan nama tidak biasa yang menimbulkan rasa malu.

sampleSentences.en: You had better check global trademark registries before launching.
sampleSentences.id: Kamu sebaiknya memeriksa daftar merek dagang global sebelum meluncurkan.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Modal verbs never take an 's' in the third person, and sentences must start with a capital letter and end with a full stop.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use 'doesn't have to' for third-person singular when expressing a lack of obligation.

mechanicsChallenges.translation: Kita sebaiknya tidak mengabaikan peraturan merek dagang.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: The expression 'had better not' must be followed by the base form of the verb without 's'.

You have to give the product a name
practicumQuestions.explanation: The phrase 'it is necessary for you to' corresponds directly to the modal structure 'You have to'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'don't have to' to show that something is optional:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is not necessary to use a family name.
targetAnswers: You don't have to use a family name.
You do not have to use a family name.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Absence of obligation is expressed using 'don't have to' or 'do not have to'.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Modal verbs like must never take an 's' ending in the third person singular.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with the correct modal of advice ('should' or 'shouldn't'):
practicumQuestions.promptText: You ________ choose a name that might fail in foreign markets.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the negative form for bad advice.
targetAnswers: You shouldn't choose a name that might fail in foreign markets.
You should not choose a name that might fail in foreign markets.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'shouldn't' or 'should not' to advise against an unwise action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the formal modal of advice 'ought to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is advisable for a brand name to be unique and memorable.
targetAnswers: A brand name ought to be unique and memorable.
A brand name ought to be unique and memorable
practicumQuestions.explanation: The formal advice structure uses 'ought to' followed by the base verb 'be'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with the strong obligation modal 'must':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Every entrepreneur ________ check trademark availability before launching.
targetAnswers: Every entrepreneur must check trademark availability before launching.
Every entrepreneur must check trademark availability before launching
practicumQuestions.explanation: Strong internal or official obligation is expressed using 'must'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the error in the infinitive particle usage after a modal verb:
practicumQuestions.promptText: You should to choose a simpler name for your application.
practicumQuestions.hint: Remove the particle 'to' after the modal verb.
targetAnswers: You should choose a simpler name for your application.
You should choose a simpler name for your application
practicumQuestions.explanation: Most modal verbs like 'should' take a bare infinitive without the word 'to'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the prohibition modal 'can't':
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is forbidden to call your twins Fish and Chips.
targetAnswers: You can't call your twins Fish and Chips.
You cannot call your twins Fish and Chips.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Strict rules and prohibitions can be expressed using 'can't' or 'cannot'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the warning using 'had better not':
practicumQuestions.promptText: You ________ ignore legal advice regarding your brand name.
targetAnswers: You had better not ignore legal advice regarding your brand name.
You'd better not ignore legal advice regarding your brand name.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Urgent negative warnings are formulated using 'had better not' followed by the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'mustn't' to express strict prohibition:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is forbidden for a name to make a fool of the child.
targetAnswers: A name mustn't make a fool of the child.
A name must not make a fool of the child.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Strict prohibitions applying to rules and regulations use 'mustn't' or 'must not'.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: What's in a Name?: Present Perfect with Already & Yet

content.summary: This speaking lab focuses on mastering the pronunciation of commercial vocabulary, sentence stress when using the present perfect with already and yet, and natural intonation patterns in professional and casual discourse.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to syllable stress shifts in derived words and sentence rhythm. When using already and yet, place auxiliary stress on the helper verb and emphasize the adverb to signal completion or expectation.

pillars.name: Syllable Stress
pillars.target: Accurate placement of primary stress in multi-syllable nouns and verbs
pillars.explanation: English relies heavily on stress-timed rhythms. Misplacing stress on words like manufacturer or advertisement can cause listener confusion.

pillars.name: Auxiliary Reduction
pillars.target: Weak forms of have and has in affirmative present perfect sentences
pillars.explanation: Native speakers typically reduce 'have' to /həv/ or /əv/ and 'has' to /həz/ or /əz/ when speaking quickly, except when emphasizing completion with already.

pillars.name: Intonation Contours
pillars.target: Rising intonation for open questions and falling intonation for definitive statements
pillars.explanation: Use falling pitch at the end of statements containing yet to express certainty about unfinished actions.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress moves from the first syllable in consumer to the second syllable in consumption.
In single root words, adding a suffix keeps the primary stress on the root syllable.
The primary stress shifts from the second syllable in advertise to the third syllable in advertisement.
The stress moves to the third syllable when changing from the base verb to the agent noun manufacturer.

drills.targetText: Have you launched the new brand logo yet?
drills.phonetic: /hæv juː lɔːntʃt ðu nuː brænd ˈləʊɡəʊ jet/
drills.focus: Present perfect question formation with yet
drills.hint: Raise your voice slightly at the end of the sentence on the word yet.

drills.targetText: She has already made a name for herself in retail.
drills.phonetic: /ʃiː hæz ɔːlˈredi meɪd ə neɪm fɔː hɜːˈself ɪn ˈriːteɪl/
drills.focus: Idiomatic phrase 'make a name for oneself' with already
drills.hint: Stress the word already clearly to emphasize that the action happened sooner than expected.

drills.targetText: The consumer has not bought from that chain yet.
drills.phonetic: /ðə kənˈsuːmər hæz nɒt bɔːt frɒm ðæt tʃeɪn jet/
drills.focus: Negative present perfect statement with yet
drills.hint: Link has and not together smoothly as hasnt.

drills.targetText: Which manufacturer created that funny advertisement?
drills.focus: Wh- question intonation and multi-syllable word stress
drills.hint: Ensure primary stress lands correctly on the third syllable of manufacturer.
